facts.claim: [Copied from notice-of-intended-marriage 03-source-pack, same source and date.] As at November 2026, the Attorney-General's Department 'Get married' page (read live 13 November 2026; page metadata updated 13 June 2024): to get married in Australia you must, among other things, 'give a notice of intended marriage form to an authorised marriage celebrant at least 1 month and no more than 18 months before your wedding' and 'be married by an authorised marriage celebrant'. The Wedded Advisor confirms current requirements.

[Copied from notice-of-intended-marriage 03-source-pack, same source and date.] As at November 2026, the Attorney-General's Department 'Get married' page (read live 13 November 2026; page metadata updated 13 June 2024): under 'Before you get married': 'complete a notice of intended marriage form' and 'give it to an authorised marriage celebrant at least 1 month (but not more than 18 months) before your wedding. Ask your authorised marriage celebrant if you need help with the form.' The Wedded Advisor confirms current requirements.

[Copied from notice-of-intended-marriage 03-source-pack, same source and date.] As at November 2026, the Attorney-General's Department 'Get married' page (read live 13 November 2026; page metadata updated 13 June 2024): 'If there is less than 1 month until your wedding, talk to your authorised marriage celebrant. You may be able to get married if a prescribed authority approves it.' Reasons listed for getting married in less than 1 month: employment-related or travel commitments; wedding or celebration arrangements; medical reasons; legal proceedings; error in giving notice. The page links 'prescribed authority' to https://marriage.ag.gov.au/stateofficers/authorities (not read in this round). The Wedded Advisor confirms current requirements.

[Copied from notice-of-intended-marriage 03-source-pack, same source and date.] As at November 2026, the Attorney-General's Department 'Get married' page (read live 13 November 2026; page metadata updated 13 June 2024): changes to the Marriage Act that became law on 12 June 2024: the option to have the NOIM witnessed remotely, via audio-visual link, as well as in person; an authorised celebrant must meet separately and in person with each party before the marriage is solemnised; re-ordering of the acceptable evidence of date and place of birth; clarifying that a NOIM can be transferred to another authorised celebrant, including at the request of the couple; clarifying that a celebrant must be physically present to solemnise a marriage, with the parties and 2 witnesses.

[Copied from notice-of-intended-marriage 03-source-pack, same source and date.] The Attorney-General's Department's Notice of Intended Marriage publication page (last updated 22 December 2022) says section 42 of the Marriage Act 1961 requires that a marriage shall not be solemnised unless a notice in writing of the intended marriage (this form) is given to the authorised celebrant solemnising the marriage. The form is downloadable as PDF and DOCX.

[Copied from notice-of-intended-marriage 03-source-pack, same source and date.] As at November 2026, Smartraveller 'Getting married overseas' (last updated 18/08/2026, read live 12 November 2026): some countries ask you to prove you aren't already married; the most common documents are a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage (CNI) and certificates from a registry of births, deaths and marriages; the country may have more rules (for example a residence period); 'We can't tell you what you will need'; contact your destination's embassy or consulate. The Wedded Advisor confirms current requirements.

[Copied from notice-of-intended-marriage 03-source-pack, same source and date.] As at November 2026, Smartraveller (read live 11 November 2026) says DFAT can issue a CNI in Australia, but some local authorities only accept CNIs issued in their country, so ask the destination's embassy or consulate whether you need a CNI, whether you can get it in Australia, and whether it also needs an authentication or apostille. The Wedded Advisor confirms current requirements.

[Copied from notice-of-intended-marriage 03-source-pack, same source and date.] Smartraveller (last updated Tuesday 18/08/2026): 'You can't register an overseas marriage in Australia. But in most cases, your marriage is legally recognised here. To be recognised, when you got married it must have been: valid under the law of the country where it happened; valid under Australian law if it had occurred in Australia.'

[Copied from name-change-after-marriage 03-source-pack, same source and date.] Australian Passport Office, 'Change of name or gender': 'If you change your family name because of a change in your marital status, you can choose to get a new passport or keep using your current one. We recommend booking travel in the name that's in your passport.' 'There are certain circumstances where we'll always need a name change certificate. This applies to any of the following: ... you were born in Australia and married or entered into a registered relationship overseas.'

[Copied from name-change-after-marriage 03-source-pack, same source and date.] Australian Passport Office: 'We'll accept foreign certificates only if you can't get an Australian equivalent because you were: born overseas; live overseas; married or entered into the relationship overseas. You must have become an Australian citizen before you entered the marriage or relationship. Foreign certificates must also be legalised. Any documents not in English need to be translated in full by an approved translation service.' Mandatory linking documents for a married name are an Australian birth or citizenship certificate plus a marriage certificate issued by an Australian RBDM, a registered relationship certificate, or an RBDM name change certificate.

[Copied from getting-married-in-seychelles 03-source-pack, same source and date.] Smartraveller (DFAT), 'How to get your documents legalised' (last updated 30/09/2026): ask the overseas authority which documents they need and which must be legalised; DFAT 'can't tell you what they may want'. Find out from the intended authority or legal representative whether you need an apostille or an authentication certificate.

[Copied from getting-married-in-seychelles 03-source-pack, same source and date.] Smartraveller: processing times vary, with delays at the end of the school year and in peak holiday periods, for incomplete requests or unpaid fees, or when the issuing authority must be contacted. An Australian-issued apostille can be verified online via DFAT.

[Copied from honeymoon-planner-cost 03-source-pack, same source and date.] Smartraveller (page last updated 18/08/2026): the right travel insurance is as essential as a passport for travel overseas; get insurance regardless of who you are, where you are going and what you are doing. The Australian Government cannot pay your bills and expects all Australians travelling overseas to take out appropriate insurance.

[Copied from honeymoon-planner-cost 03-source-pack, same source and date.] Smartraveller: always declare everything upfront when you buy a policy, or you may void it; you must tell your insurer about all pre-existing health conditions.

[Copied from honeymoon-planner-cost 03-source-pack, same source and date.] Smartraveller travel insurance buying guide: if a circumstance, risk or event is known before you buy the policy, you will not be covered if it directly affects your travel. The earlier you buy travel insurance, the more likely you are to be covered if something unexpected happens at your destination before your trip.

insider_details.detail: Lodge the Notice of Intended Marriage early in the plan, since it must reach your authorised celebrant at least 1 month and no more than 18 months before the wedding. Shortening of time is only possible if a prescribed authority approves it.

For an overseas wedding, ask the destination's embassy or consulate early whether you need a Certificate of No Impediment, where it must be issued, and whether it needs an apostille, because legalisation processing times vary and slow down at peak holiday periods.
Book honeymoon flights in the name on your current passport. Changing your passport name after marriage is optional, and the Passport Office recommends booking travel in the passport name.
Buy travel insurance as soon as you book the wedding and honeymoon travel: events known before purchase are not covered, and the earlier you buy, the more likely you are to be covered.
